Problem: How do you abandon laziness and cultivate aroused energy?
Context: A practitioner finds themselves experiencing various physical or mental conditions, such as having work to do, having completed work, preparing for a journey, or having finished a journey, which trigger thoughts of fatigue and a desire to lie down.
This leads to a lack of effort for attaining the as-yet-unattained, reaching the as-yet-unreached, or realizing the as-yet-unrealized, thereby hindering spiritual progress.

Similarly, situations like not getting enough almsfood, getting too much almsfood (leading to bodily heaviness), experiencing a slight illness, or recovering from an illness are perceived as justifications for resting, further obstructing diligent practice.
The mind, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, is prone to such inclinations, lacking the pliancy and development needed to overcome these obstacles and make strenuous effort.

This pattern is applicable when a monk in training struggles with maintaining persistence and alertness in the face of daily tasks, physical states, or a general tendency towards idleness, risking decline in skillful qualities.
Forces: The body's natural inclination towards comfort and aversion to exertion, particularly after or during work, travel, or illness, acts as a powerful countervailing force, making it difficult to maintain spiritual effort.

The mind's inherent tendency to be 'quick to reverse itself' and its 'undeveloped' and 'unpliant' nature contribute to laziness, making it hard to sustain concentration and develop skillful qualities.
The allure of immediate sensual gratification and the satisfaction of physical ease often overshadow the long-term benefits of rigorous practice, leading to complacency and a 'slack going-forth'.

A failure to properly discern the 'origination, the passing away, the allure, the drawbacks, & the escape' from the six media of contact means that a monk may not see the danger in giving in to sloth and torpor, or in delighting in attachment.

The tendency to 'fall back on what was done in the past as being essential' or to be consumed by 'delusion-born fevers' can undermine the desire and effort to cultivate new, skillful qualities, perpetuating the cycle of laziness.

The complexity of the path to awakening and the subtle nature of hindrances, such as the 'tangled skein' of craving, make a simple 'fix' insufficient, requiring consistent, ardent, and resolute effort to unravel these defilements.

Scope:
Eight grounds for laziness: There is the case, friends, where a monk has some work to do. The thought occurs to him: 'I will have to do this work. But when I have done this work, my body will be tired. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the first ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk has done some work. The thought occurs to him: 'I have done some work. Now that I have done work, my body is tired. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the second ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk has to go on a journey. The thought occurs to him: 'I will have to go on this journey. But when I have gone on the journey, my body will be tired. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the third ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk has gone on a journey. The thought occurs to him: 'I have gone on a journey. Now that I have gone on a journey, my body is tired. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the fourth ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk, having gone for alms in a village or town, does not get as much coarse or refined food as he would like for his fill. The thought occurs to him: 'I, having gone for alms in a village or town, have not gotten as much coarse or refined food as I would like for my fill. This body of mine is tired & unsuitable for work. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the fifth ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk, having gone for alms in a village or town, gets as much coarse or refined food as he would like for his fill. The thought occurs to him: 'I, having gone for alms in a village or town, have gotten as much coarse or refined food as I would like for my fill. This body of mine is heavy & unsuitable for work—stuffed with beans, as it were. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the sixth ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk comes down with a slight illness. The thought occurs to him: 'I have come down with a slight illness. There's a need to lie down.' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the seventh ground for laziness.

'Then there is the case where a monk has recovered from his illness, not long after his recovery. The thought occurs to him: 'I have recovered from my illness. It's not long after my recovery. This body of mine is weak & unsuitable for work. Why don't I lie down?' So he lies down. He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the eighth ground for laziness.

'Monks, six qualities lead to the decline of a monk in training. Which six? Delighting in work, delighting in talking, delighting in sleeping, delighting in entanglement, not guarding the sense faculties, not knowing moderation in food. These six qualities lead to the decline of a monk in training.
'Young, strong, but lethargic, the resolves of his heart exhausted, the lazy, lethargic one loses the path to discernment.

'Monks, endowed with six qualities, a monk is incapable of attaining what is to be witnessed right there whenever there is an opening. Which six?

'There is the case where a monk doesn't discern as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in decline.' He doesn't discern as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in stability.' He doesn't discern as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in distinction.' He doesn't discern as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in penetration.' He is one who doesn't act attentively. He is one who doesn't act suitably.

'Monks, endowed with six qualities, a monk is capable of attaining what is to be witnessed right there whenever there is an opening. Which six?

'There is the case where a monk discerns as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in decline.' He discerns as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in stability.' He discerns as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in distinction.' He discerns as it has come to be that 'This quality has a share in penetration.' He is one who acts attentively. He is one who acts suitably.

Eight grounds for the arousal of energy: There is the case, friends, where a monk has some work to do. The thought occurs to him: 'I will have to do this work. But when I am doing this work, it will not be easy to attend to the Buddha's message. Why don't I make an effort beforehand for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?' So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the first ground for the arousal of energy.

Without abandoning these five qualities, one is incapable of entering & remaining in the first jhāna… incapable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry… the fruit of once-returning… the fruit of non-returning… arahantship. Which five? Stinginess as to one's monastery (lodgings)… one's family (of supporters)… one's gains… one's status, and ingratitude. Without abandoning these five qualities, one is incapable of entering & remaining in the second jhāna… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna; one is incapable realizing the fruit of stream-entry… the fruit of once-returning… the fruit of non-returning… arahantship.

The repeated phrase 'he doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained...' in the context of 'Eight grounds for laziness' [DN_nblm.txt 151] clearly establishes 'laziness' as the 'enter from' state. The pattern name itself further reinforces this.
Laziness, characterised by lack of effort in the face of various circumstances, is established as the primary 'enter from' state, preventing spiritual attainment.

The 'Eight grounds for the arousal of energy' are presented as the direct counter to the 'Eight grounds for laziness,' indicating that 'aroused energy' is the desired 'exit to' state. This represents the successful overcoming of idleness to pursue spiritual goals.
Aroused energy, manifested as making effort for the un-attained, is the natural 'exit to' state, directly opposing the passive 'lying down' described in the laziness grounds.

The `answerExcerpt` explicitly describes actions of 'a monk'. Furthermore, references to 'monk in training' and the broader context of the Dhamma indicate that these patterns apply to practitioners who are still developing and have not yet reached full awakening. This aligns with 'conviction-dhamma-follower', 'stream-enterer', and 'once-returner'.

The grounds for laziness are directly applicable to 'monks in training', implying that those who have not yet reached full awakening (arahantship) are the target audience, specifically encompassing 'conviction-dhamma-follower', 'stream-enterer', and 'once-returner'.
Problem: 'abandon' is used to express moving away from the negative state of laziness. 'cultivate aroused energy' is used to express the desired outcome of the effort, aligning with the positive counterpart 'grounds for the arousal of energy' from the sources. 'cultivate' is chosen to reflect the active development required, consistent with the effort described in the sources.
Context: The description of the 'Eight grounds for laziness' directly outlines the various situations (work, journey, alms, illness) where a monk's body feels tired or heavy, leading to the decision to 'lie down' instead of making effort. This forms the primary symptom of the problem.
The phrase 'He doesn't make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained...' explicitly states the consequence of this inaction, linking it to a lack of spiritual progress.

Quotations such as the mind being 'untamed, unguarded, unprotected, unrestrained' and thus leading to 'great harm', or being 'undeveloped' and 'unpliant', directly describe the internal mental state that makes the practitioner susceptible to these grounds for laziness.

The inclusion of 'getting as much coarse or refined food as he would like for his fill' making the body 'heavy & unsuitable for work' and the phrase 'Luminous, monks, is the mind. And it is defiled by incoming defilements. The uninstructed run-of-the-mill person doesn't discern that as it has come to be, which is why I tell you that—for the uninstructed run-of-the-mill person—there is no development of the mind.' further characterise the 'diagnosis' of a mind easily influenced by external conditions and lacking discernment.

The overall context of 'decline of a monk in training' and the applicability to 'monks in training' supports the framing as a 'medical prescription' for those experiencing these symptoms of laziness and lack of effort.
Forces: The detailed description of the 'Eight grounds for laziness' themselves inherently describes the internal and external pressures that pull the practitioner towards inaction, directly opposing sustained effort. This is the core conflict.

The mind's inherent 'unpliancy' when undeveloped and its characteristic of being 'quick to reverse itself' means that even a good intention can easily be overridden by the desire for ease, making a simple resolution insufficient.

The 'delight in attachment' to sensual pleasures and physical comfort provides a strong 'allure' that distracts from the deeper spiritual goal, making the path of ease seem more attractive than the effortful path. Similarly, 'delighting in sleeping' as a quality of decline highlights this force.

The 'tangled skein' of craving and the general difficulty for a 'generation delighting in attachment' to see 'conditionality & dependent co-arising' implies a lack of deep insight into the long-term consequences of laziness, thus making it hard to abandon without a structured approach.

The tendency to 'fall back on what was done in the past as being essential' creates a powerful inertia, suppressing the 'desire' and 'effort' to initiate or continue skillful actions, making the transition from laziness to aroused energy intrinsically challenging.

The concept of 'delusion-born fevers' and the observation that 'the lazy, lethargic one loses the path to discernment' indicates that mental obscurations actively work against the cultivation of energy and clear seeing, highlighting the need for a nuanced solution.
